newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Summit aims to shape Caribbean's future.
newsitem.headline: Summit aims to shape Caribbean's future.

text.p: Heads of government of the 14-member Caribbean Community (Caricom) begin a summit meeting on Monday which regional leaders hope will prove one of their most important since the regional trade bloc was created 24 years ago.

The leaders are expected to approve treaty amendments aimed at establishing the region as a single market by the year 1999, as well as beginning the process toward creating a single economy and common currency. The meeting will be held in the resort town of Montego Bay Monday through Friday.
The summit also will consider membership applications from Haiti and the British Virgin Islands, which if approved would double Caricom's population.

A single market and economy has been a long-standing Caricom goal first articulated in 1989. Several deadlines for its creation were set -- and broken -- but regional officials now say the 1999 deadline is feasible.

A common external tariff is on schedule for full implementation this year. Non-tariff barriers remain on six products, but Caricom Secretary-General Edwin Carrington said, "I am hoping to remove three or four of them at this summit."

The free movement of skilled labour has been implemented by eight Caricom states, while double taxation provisions exist in seven. The treaty amendments to be signed will allow Caricom companies and individuals to establish investments freely in any country, and be given equal treatment as if they were nationals of that country.

Carrington said these amendments are the second in a series of eight that will define the Caricom single market and economy. Future protocols will cover transportation, industrial policy, fiscal and monetary policy, dispute settlements and continued preferences for Caricom's smaller member-states.
"It is an attempt to better organise ourselves to exploit and defend our advantages in the international economy," Carrington explained.
The region will also consider membership applications from the British Virgin Islands and Haiti. The acceptance of the latter would mark a major policy shift within Caricom.

The 1992 report of the independent West Indian Commission, established by Caricom, stated with regard to widening Caricom's membership that it had to be done "without being overwhelmed by new members and end up being lost in our own widened community."

It was for this reason that Caricom spearheaded the creation of the 24-nation Association of Caribbean States in 1995, of which Haiti is a member. But political realities, such as the imminent commencement of talks for a Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA), have forced Caricom to revisit its decision to limit Caricom's membership.

The admission of Haiti would boost the region's population from 6 million to 12 million overnight. However, it would also create logistical problems that officials admit may not be resolved at this summit.

With the exception of Surinam, all Caricom member-states are English-speaking and English is the sole official language. One senior official said the addition of French as a working language would place huge strains on Caricom's already limited budget.

In addition, there are concerns about the recent political instability in that country, the differences in the legal systems, as well as Haiti's ability to hit the ground running with regard to work toward a single market.

The summit is expected to mandate a fact-finding mission being sent to Haiti to assess the possibilities of Haiti's accession. President Rene Preval will be at the summit, along with the Dominican Republic's Lionel Fernandez, to discuss the region's joint negotiations regarding the extension of the Lome trade and aid accord with the European Union, and the FTAA.
Caricom will also consider a proposal from Cuba to sign a free trade accord with Havana.
Some, such as Guyana and Trinidad, are pushing for negotiations to begin, while officials in Grenada and Jamaica have voiced the need to move cautiously.
